offlineReplay.renderedText:
A full week in Yellowstone lets you do the whole Grand Loop without rushing — this route circles the park counterclockwise, hitting all five major basins plus wildlife country up north.

 Day 1 — Arrival & Upper Geyser Basin
Ease into the park at Old Faithful — it's the classic first stop and the visitor center staff there track live eruption predictions, so you're not guessing.
   Old Faithful Visitor Education Center
  Check the eruption prediction board and grab a basin map — this is your orientation point for the day.
   Old Faithful
  Eruptions usually run every 60–110 minutes and last 1.5–5 minutes. Arrive 20 minutes early and grab a bench seat.
   Upper Geyser Basin Boardwalk Loop
  ~2.4mi flat boardwalk loop, Easy, ~1.5hrs. Passes Morning Glory Pool and Castle Geyser — the highest concentration of geysers on Earth.
   Old Faithful Inn Dining Room
  Dinner in the historic log lodge — reservations recommended, it fills fast in summer.
   Old Faithful Inn or Snow Lodge
  Overnight near the geyser basin.

 Day 2 — West Thumb & Grand Loop South
Short, easy morning at the lake, then a slow wildlife-watching drive into Hayden Valley before landing at Canyon for the night.
   West Thumb Geyser Basin
  ~0.5mi boardwalk loop, Easy. Geysers steaming right at the edge of Yellowstone Lake — unusual and photogenic combo.
   Yellowstone Lake Overlook Trail
  ~2mi loop, Moderate, some elevation. Quiet views over the lake, usually far less crowded than the basin boardwalks.
   Lake Yellowstone Hotel
  Lunch stop at the historic yellow hotel on the lakeshore.
   Hayden Valley
  Prime bison and often wolf/grizzly territory — pull-offs are the move, especially in the evening light.
   Canyon Lodge & Cabins
  Overnight near the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone.

 Day 3 — Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone
This is the visual heavyweight day — plan for a slower pace with two solid hikes and one epic overlook.
   Artist Point
  Short paved walk, Easy. The iconic view of Lower Falls — go early to beat the crowds.
   Uncle Tom's Trail
  ~0.5mi round trip, ~500ft descent on metal stairs, Strenuous despite the short distance. Puts you right at the base of the falls.
   North Rim Trail (Brink of Lower Falls)
  ~1.5mi one-way segment, Moderate. Close-up views of the falls thundering over the edge.
   Canyon Lodge Eatery
  Easy lunch or dinner stop, casual cafeteria-style.
   Mount Washburn area viewpoint
  Drive-up viewpoint with wide views of the canyon country and, often, bighorn sheep on the slopes.
   Canyon Lodge & Cabins
  Second night here.

 Day 4 — Lamar Valley & Northeast Wildlife
Head northeast for the best wildlife odds in the park — bring binoculars and get moving early.
   Lamar Valley
  Yellowstone's "American Serengeti" — wolves, bison herds, and pronghorn are most active at dawn.
   Tower Fall
  Short overlook walk, Easy. A 132ft waterfall visible right from the trail.
   Slough Creek Trail (out-and-back segment)
  ~4mi round trip to the first meadow, Moderate. One of the best wolf-watching spots in the park.
   Roosevelt Lodge area
  Old West atmosphere, lunch, and horseback ride options if you want to break up the driving.
   Mammoth Hot Springs Hotel
  Overnight in the north.

 Day 5 — Mammoth Hot Springs & Norris
A geology-heavy day — travertine terraces in the morning, the park's most volatile basin in the afternoon.
   Mammoth Hot Springs Terraces (Upper & Lower)
  Boardwalk loops, Easy. Otherworldly limestone terraces that shift shape year to year.
   Sheepeater Cliff
  Quick roadside stop — columnar basalt formations, good for stretching your legs.
   Norris Geyser Basin Loop (Porcelain & Back Basin)
  ~3mi combined, Moderate. Hottest, most acidic, most unpredictable basin in the park.
   Norris area picnic area
  Lunch break before the drive back south.
   Canyon Lodge & Cabins
  Back to Canyon for the night.

 Day 6 — Midway Basin & Yellowstone Lake
Back down to the geyser country for the park's most photographed feature, plus a real hike to earn a waterfall.
   Grand Prismatic Spring Overlook Trail
  ~1.6mi round trip with a short climb, Moderate. The overlook is what makes the colors pop — skipping it means missing the shot everyone knows.
   Fountain Paint Pot
  ~0.5mi loop, Easy. Bubbling mud pots and small geysers in a tight, easy walk.
   Old Faithful Lodge Cafeteria
  Casual lunch back near Old Faithful.
   Fairy Falls Trail
  ~5–6mi round trip, Moderate, mostly flat. Leads to a 200ft waterfall — usually much quieter than the basin boardwalks.
   Old Faithful Snow Lodge
  Final overnight in the park.

 Day 7 — Final Geysers & Departure
One last eruption, one more boardwalk, then head out.
   Old Faithful
  Catch a final eruption before packing up — worth checking the prediction board one more time.
   Biscuit Basin Boardwalk
  ~0.5mi loop, Easy. Sapphire Pool and Black Opal Pool make a low-key finale.
   Depart via West or South Entrance
  West Entrance runs toward Bozeman/West Yellowstone; South Entrance runs toward Jackson and Grand Teton — pick based on your flight out.

## At a glance
- August is Yellowstone's busiest stretch, so parking lots at Old Faithful, Grand Prismatic, and Canyon typically fill by mid-morning — aim to hit marquee stops before 9am or after 4pm.
- In-park lodges (Old Faithful Inn, Canyon Lodge, Mammoth Hot Springs Hotel) usually book out 6-12 months ahead for summer — if you don't have reservations yet, West Yellowstone or Gardiner as gateway towns are the fallback.
- The Grand Loop Road is roughly 140 miles total; this route breaks it into manageable daily legs of 1-2.5 hours of driving rather than one long slog.
- Wildlife jams are real — budget extra time whenever you're in Hayden or Lamar Valley, traffic can stop for bison crossing the road.
- Cell coverage is spotty to nonexistent through most of the interior — download offline maps before you go.

Worth a quick look at current alerts for [Yellowstone on TrailVerse](https://www.nationalparksexplorerusa.com/parks/yellowstone?tab=alerts) before you go, since road and facility conditions can shift.

## Don't Forget
- Bear spray (rentable in West Yellowstone or Gardiner) if you're doing Slough Creek or Fairy Falls
- Binoculars for Lamar/Hayden wildlife watching
- Layers — mornings in the 40s even in August, afternoons can hit 80
- Sturdy shoes for boardwalks and the Uncle Tom's Trail stairs
- Park entrance fee is typically $35/vehicle for 7 days, or use an America the Beautiful annual pass
